pairs.rationale: Both identify Lazarus at Bethany in Jesus' narrative. John11 introduces his illness and his sisters; John12 explicitly recalls his raising. This links the same named household without identifying him with Luke's parable Lazarus or independently establishing every biographical detail.

The narrator identifies Mary through the foot anointing and hair wiping that the later chapter narrates. The action and person are explicit in both; the later event is not imported as already occurring during Lazarus's illness.

The sisters describe Lazarus as the one Jesus loves; later onlookers respond to Jesus' tears by saying how He loved him. The speakers and moments differ, and their statements are not independent proof of every illness or grief detail.

Both connect this raising account with seeing or displaying God's glory. The earlier statement names the illness's purpose and the Son's glorification; the later answer to Martha names belief and seeing glory. Their audience and exact conditions are not equated.

The narrator's statement that Jesus loved Lazarus corresponds to the sisters' earlier description of him as the one Jesus loves. The narrator additionally names His love for Martha and Mary, which the earlier message does not separately repeat.

Jesus' proposed return to Judea is immediately taken up in the disciples' objection to going there again after threatened stoning. This makes the stated destination and its narrated risk explicit, without treating the reply as another journey or independent attestation.

The disciples recall attempted stoning; the earlier controversy explicitly narrates stones taken up against Jesus and the ensuing exchange. The earlier units supply that danger, not the disciples' later objection or an independent date for it.

Both connect walking in available light with avoiding darkness's danger. John11 uses daytime and twelve hours; John12 describes the Light's remaining presence. The different settings and temporal images are preserved.
Both portray walking in darkness as impaired movement. John11 says stumbling because light is not in the person; John12 says not knowing where one goes. Neither sentence is substituted for the other.

Both raising narratives use sleep language for someone whose death is at issue. John later explicitly explains Lazarus's sleep as death; Mark has Jesus say the girl is sleeping rather than dead. The persons, wording and events remain distinct.

The disciples infer recovery from ordinary sleep; the narrator explicitly contrasts their resting-in-sleep understanding with Jesus' reference to death. This is the story's own explanation, not an independent medical account.

The narrator says Jesus meant death, and the following direct statement openly says Lazarus died. The link clarifies the sleep wording without inventing a death occurring between Jesus' two statements.

Jesus' direct Lazarus-died statement explains His earlier description of the friend falling asleep and His intention to awaken him. The earlier sleep wording is retained rather than changed into a different condition or timeline.

Both give the raising episode a stated belief-directed purpose. Jesus addresses disciples about His absence for their sake; later He explains His spoken prayer for the crowd's belief in His sending. The groups and means differ.

Both express willingness to die with Jesus. Thomas urges fellow disciples to go and die with Him; Mark records Peter's insistence and others agreeing before the arrest. Speakers, moments and the added denial language remain distinct.

The four-day tomb notice is repeated in Martha's warning that there is already a smell after four days. This connects the narrator's duration with her stated concern without adding a medical explanation or a new burial chronology.
Both describe the people consoling Mary and Martha over their brother. The later verse follows those with Mary as she leaves; it does not independently attest every earlier arrival or number.
Martha hears Jesus is coming and goes to meet Him; Mary later hears the summons and rises quickly to come. Their responses occur at different moments, and Mary's initial staying home is not erased.

Martha and Mary each tell Jesus that their brother would not have died had He been there. The repeated saying is an explicit literary counterpart; Mary's falling at His feet belongs to her later scene.

Martha expresses confidence that God answers Jesus; Jesus later thanks the Father for hearing Him and says He always hears. Martha's confidence and Jesus' thanksgiving have different speakers and forms, and neither is turned into a newly supplied divine promise or a record of an unreported petition.

Jesus' promise that the brother will rise is followed by His call to Lazarus and the dead man's emergence. The later account supplies the concrete raising, not Martha's initial interpretation of its timing.

Both explicitly speak of raising on the last day. Martha applies that expectation to her brother; Jesus' earlier teaching speaks of those given to Him and those beholding and believing the Son. The individual expectation and broader promises remain distinct.

Both connect believing in Jesus/the Son with life and resurrection. John11 calls Jesus resurrection and life even across death; John6 promises eternal life and last-day raising. Their exact descriptions and time language are preserved.

Both promise not beholding or undergoing death in relation to Jesus. John11 names living and believing; John8 names keeping His word. The conditions and expressions are not made verbatim or turned into an unsupported claim that every believer avoids bodily death.
Both confess Jesus as the Christ and God's Son. Martha additionally names the One coming into the world; Peter says Son of the living God. The speakers and occasions are not identified.

Both convey to another person that Jesus calls them. Martha secretly tells Mary the Teacher is here and calls; the crowd encourages the blind man that Jesus is calling. Recipients, messengers and circumstances differ.
Mary quickly rises and goes after hearing the summons, corresponding to Martha's earlier going to meet Jesus upon hearing His arrival. The two sisters and the different messages remain distinct.

The people consoling Mary are the same narrative's previously introduced consolers of the sisters. The earlier notice does not independently report their following her or their mistaken assumption about a tomb visit.
Mary's conditional statement about Jesus' presence and her brother's death repeats Martha's earlier words. Mary also falls at His feet; that gesture is not assigned to Martha's statement.

Both describe Jesus being troubled in spirit. The raising scene also names indignation while people weep; the supper scene introduces His betrayal announcement. The causes, occasions and additional emotions are different.
Both explicitly narrate Jesus weeping. John places the tears in Lazarus's mourning scene; Luke places them at the sight of Jerusalem. The objects and circumstances of grief are not equated.

The onlookers' statement about Jesus loving Lazarus recalls the sisters' description of the ill man as the one He loves. Different speakers interpret different moments; the earlier message does not independently narrate these tears.

The onlookers recall opening a blind man's eyes; the earlier Johannine account narrates Jesus' mud-and-washing healing followed by sight. That account supplies a concrete counterpart to the recalled deed, not the later claim about preventing Lazarus's death or a list of every witness.

Both raising accounts describe a stone at a tomb. Lazarus's cave still has its stone before the removal command; Jesus' tomb is found with its stone already removed. The tombs, deceased persons and narrative stages are different.
Martha's four-day warning recalls the narrator's four-day tomb notice at Jesus' arrival. The earlier unit supports the stated duration, not an independent sensory or medical report of the smell.

The promise of seeing God's glory returns to the earlier statement that the illness serves God's glory and the Son's glorification. John11:4 does not name Martha as the original hearer or reproduce the later conditional belief wording.

Both describe Jesus lifting His eyes heavenward and addressing Father. Here He thanks for being heard before the raising; John17 opens the hour-and-glory prayer. Their requests, responses and settings remain distinct.

Both prayers connect hearers' belief with the Father's sending Jesus. Here Jesus explains His public words for the crowd; John17 describes disciples receiving His words and believing the sending. The crowd, disciples and reported stages of belief differ.

Jesus' call into Lazarus's tomb provides a specific example to compare with His teaching that those in tombs will hear His voice and come out. One raising does not complete John5's universal future resurrection or its contrasting outcomes.

Both accounts describe burial cloths including a face cloth. Lazarus emerges still bound and Jesus tells those present to unbind and release him; Peter finds Jesus' linen lying and face cloth separately wrapped. The addressees, states of the cloths and raising narratives are not made identical.

Both narrate many people believing after seeing Jesus' signs or deed. John11 concerns witnesses with Mary after Lazarus's raising; John2 concerns Jerusalem's feast signs. Neither account independently counts the other's converts or establishes identical quality of belief.

Both narrate people reporting a healing deed to religious interlocutors before opposition intensifies. John11 has some witnesses inform Pharisees; John5 has the restored man identify Jesus to the Jews. The reporters, methods and unspoken motives are not equated.

Both describe religious leaders gathering before a death plot against Jesus. Matthew names the high priest Caiaphas and chief priests/elders; John names chief priests/Pharisees and their acknowledgment of many signs. Their meetings, speeches and stages are not declared identical.

The later trial narration identifies Caiaphas as high priest that year and recalls his advice about one person dying for the people. This is the same named counselor's explicit narrative return, not independent evidence for every institutional detail.
John18 explicitly recalls Caiaphas's better-for-one-person-to-die advice given here. The later summary does not reproduce the whole nation-perishing contrast or create a separate independent witness.

The narrator interprets Caiaphas's preceding one-for-the-people advice as prophecy of Jesus' death for the nation. The hostile counselor's words and the narrator's explanation are distinguished; no unreported understanding of the prophecy is assigned to Caiaphas.

Both describe Jesus' people brought into one collective. John11 names scattered children of God beyond the nation; John10 names other sheep and one flock/shepherd. The metaphors are related without identifying every group with an unstated nation or assigning individuals by analogy.

Both narrate leaders planning Jesus' death. John dates the decision from the Lazarus council; Mark introduces the plot when the feasts are two days away. No single meeting date or identical sequence is imposed.

Both describe Jesus withdrawing after danger of seizure. John11 names Ephraim near wilderness and the disciples; John10 names escape and retreat beyond the Jordan. The places and journeys are not equated.

Both connect approaching Passover with going up to Jerusalem. John11 concerns pilgrims coming beforehand to purify themselves; John2 narrates Jesus going. Travelers, purification details and visits remain distinct.

Both describe uncertainty and searching for Jesus at a feast. John11 concerns the approaching Passover and temple speculation; John7 concerns His initially secret arrival at Booths. Feasts, locations of speech and journeys are not merged.
Both name chief priests and Pharisees seeking to seize Jesus. John11 gives a location-reporting order; John7 describes sending officers after hearing crowd talk. The orders and moments differ.

The introduction explicitly recalls the raising of Lazarus that the earlier chapter narrates through the call and emergence. The six-days-before-Passover arrival notice belongs here rather than to the earlier raising account.

Both describe Martha serving in Jesus' presence. Luke adds distraction and a complaint about her sister; John names Lazarus reclining at this supper without that complaint. The visits and Luke's unnamed village are not identified with one dated meal.

Both describe costly genuine/pure nard used to anoint Jesus in a Bethany meal setting. John names Mary, a litra, feet and hair; Mark names an unnamed woman, a broken alabaster jar, head and Simon the leper's house. Different details and chronology are preserved without supplying an identity or date.

Both name Judas Iscariot among Jesus' disciples/Twelve and connect him with handing Jesus over. John makes him the perfume objection's speaker; Mark14:10 does not independently identify the unnamed critics of its earlier meal scene.

Both object that the perfume could have been sold and its price given to the poor. John names Judas and three hundred denarii; Mark names some objectors and more than three hundred. The speakers and amounts remain distinct.

Both identify Judas with the money box. John12's narrator calls him a thief and rejects a poor-care motive; John13 reports disciples' guesses about purchases or charity. The repeated role does not turn their guesses into the narrator's judgment or independently prove the theft.

Both defend the woman and connect her act with Jesus' burial. John says leave her so she may keep it for His burial day; Mark says she already anointed His body beforehand. Those formulations and Mark's additional good-work praise are not harmonized.
Both contrast the poor always being with the hearers with Jesus not always being present. Mark additionally permits doing them good whenever desired.

The later crowd comes also to see the raised Lazarus; the earlier scene narrates his emergence and witnesses believing. These are responses to the same named raising, without identifying the arriving crowd with every earlier eyewitness or adding a second raising.

The earlier decision targets Jesus; the later chief-priest plot targets Lazarus also. The explicit extension of danger is compared without identifying the two victims or narrating the second plan as carried out.

Both relate belief in Jesus to Lazarus's raising. The earlier notice names people who saw it with Mary; the later notice explains the plot through people going away and believing on Lazarus's account. The groups and stages are not automatically identical.

Both place a public crowd reception at Jesus' Jerusalem approach. John introduces a feast crowd hearing of His arrival before the next unit's acclamation; Mark describes garments, branches and those ahead/behind acclaiming Him. The next-day and feast-participant details are not supplied from Mark.

The crowd's blessing of the One coming in the Lord's name corresponds to the psalm's blessing. John adds Hosanna, King of Israel and palm branches in the entry narrative; the psalm adds blessing from the Lord's house.

Both describe Jesus seated on a colt. John says He found a young donkey and introduces Scripture; Mark says disciples brought the colt and put garments on it. The means of obtaining it are not merged.

Both announce Zion's coming king mounted on the animal. John says Do not fear and a donkey's colt; Zechariah says Rejoice/proclaim and a beast of burden and young colt, adding righteous, saving and gentle. The actual supplied animal and introductory wording remain distinct.

Both recount disciples later remembering Scripture or Jesus' words. John12 says after His glorification concerning entry actions; John2 says after His resurrection concerning the temple saying. The remembered content and time formulations are not made identical.

The entry narrative explicitly recalls the crowd present when Jesus called Lazarus from the tomb. The earlier passage narrates that call and emergence; it does not independently narrate the later testimony or identify every witness.

The crowd's meeting Jesus because it heard of the sign follows the earlier eyewitness crowd's testimony about Lazarus. The narrative connects the same sign with testimony and reception; eyewitnesses and hearers are not automatically one group.

Both report authorities treating widespread belief in Jesus as their problem. John12's Pharisees say the world went after Him; John11's speakers fear everyone believing and Roman action. Their rhetoric is not an independently verified worldwide conversion count.

Greeks going up to worship can be compared with Isaiah's foreigners attached to the Lord and welcome in His prayer house for all nations. John does not specify these individuals' circumcision, Sabbath or covenant status, or declare this group complete fulfillment of the promise.

Both identify Philip with Bethsaida in Galilee's ministry context. John12 additionally records Greeks' request to see Jesus; John1 describes Philip's call and the town shared with Andrew and Peter, without independently narrating that request.

Both announce the Son of Man's glorification. John12 says the hour has come; John13 says now after Judas leaves and names God's reciprocal glorification. Their temporal markers and explanatory clauses are preserved.

Both use a sown grain's death before subsequent life or fruit. Jesus speaks of wheat no longer remaining alone but bearing much fruit; Paul discusses the resurrection body's relation to bare seed and God's giving a body. The images serve different expositions, not one literal botanical or resurrection timetable.

Both contrast preserving life by surrender with losing it through attachment to present life. John says loving/hating one's life in this world and keeping it for eternal life; Mark names losing it for Jesus and the gospel. The supplied verbs and qualifications remain distinct.

Both promise Jesus' followers a place with Him where He is. John12 speaks of the servant following Him and the Father's honor; John14 speaks of preparing and receiving them. Those additional promises and their formulations differ.

Both portray Jesus deeply troubled while facing His hour. John poses whether to ask rescue and affirms His purpose in reaching the hour; Mark quotes the cup-removal request and submission to the Father's will. The public discourse and Gethsemane scene are not relocated or made verbally identical.

Both address Father and request glorification in the hour's context. John12 asks glory for the Father's name and receives a heavenly reply; John17 asks the Son's glorification so He may glorify the Father. The request objects and response narration remain distinct.

Both have Jesus explain spoken revelation as benefiting the surrounding hearers. Here the heavenly voice is for them; earlier Jesus speaks His own prayer so the crowd may believe His sending. The vocal agents and events are not equated.

Both connect judgment with the ruler of this world. John12 says now judgment and the ruler will be cast out; John16 says the ruler has been judged. No unnamed earthly ruler or single reconciled tense is substituted.

Both speak of the Son of Man/Jesus being lifted up with a life-giving result. John3 adds Moses' lifted snake and faith unto life; John12 says drawing all to Himself, with the narrator next explaining death. Those images and effects remain distinct.

Both narrator comments describe Jesus' words as indicating the kind of death He would die. John18 adds the handover dialogue and fulfillment language. It recalls the earlier death indication without independently verifying every legal claim made by the speakers.

The crowd's Son-of-Man question and expectation of lasting messianic rule can be compared with Daniel's son-of-man figure and everlasting authority/kingdom. Daniel does not verbatim say Christ cannot die, and its actual Greek-based Ancient-of-Days formulation is not replaced with another edition's wording.

Both connect available light with safe walking and darkness with impaired movement. John12 names the Light's short remaining presence and not knowing one's direction; John11 names day, night and stumbling. Their images and time descriptions are not identical.

Both associate the hearers with sons of light. John commands belief in the Light toward that status; Paul affirms it and urges watchfulness and sobriety. The withdrawal of Jesus belongs only to John's narrative.

Both explicitly deny that seeing Jesus or His signs necessarily produced belief among the stated hearers. The narrator here names many signs; John6 quotes Jesus about having seen Him. This does not erase the same Gospel's other accounts of people believing.

John quotes the report-unbelieved and Lord's-arm-revealed questions from Isaiah. The application to this unbelief is John's narrative explanation; Isaiah's unit does not name the particular Gospel hearers.

John introduces Isaiah's blindness/heart saying as the reason they could not believe, then quotes it next. The target supplies the relevant imagery while retaining its own heart-grown-dull and self-closed-eyes formulation rather than John's active He wording.

Both concern eyes, heart, turning and healing. John says He blinded and hardened; the supplied Isaiah says the people's heart grew dull, ears heard heavily and they closed their eyes. The agency, hearing clause and sentence forms are preserved rather than harmonized.

Isaiah narrates seeing the enthroned Lord and speaks of His glory filling house and earth. John applies Isaiah's seeing and speaking to Jesus' glory. The identification is John's stated application; Isaiah's vision is not rewritten to contain Jesus' name or a new independent identification.

Both describe fear of synagogue expulsion related to confessing Jesus as Christ. John12 concerns rulers who believed without confessing; John9 concerns the healed man's parents. Their knowledge, statements and groups remain distinct.

Both oppose human glory to God's glory in the reception of Jesus. John12 explains rulers' hidden belief; John5 asks how people can believe while seeking each other's glory. Belief-without-confession and the earlier question are not silently made identical.

Both connect belief in Jesus with belief in God or His Sender. John12 says not in Me but in the One who sent Me; John14 commands belief in God and also in Me. The distinct formulations are retained rather than removing either Jesus or the Father from the statements.

Both connect beholding Jesus with beholding the Father or Sender. John14 addresses Philip's request and explicitly names the Father; John12 states the shorter Sender formulation. No collapse of the speakers or roles is inferred.

Both call Jesus Light in the world and connect response to Him with escape from darkness. John12 names believing and not remaining in darkness; John8 names following and having life's light. The conditions remain their supplied words.

Both distinguish Jesus' saving mission from judging the world. John12 has Jesus describe His coming while addressing hearers who do not keep His words; John3 describes God's sending the Son. Their agents and additional clauses remain distinct.

Both relate response to Jesus' word to judgment. John12 warns of rejection and the word judging on the last day; John5 promises the hearer who believes the Sender does not come into judgment. The opposing responses and exact time language are not erased.

Both deny speaking from Jesus Himself and refer His words to the Father. John12 describes a command concerning what to say; John14 describes the indwelling Father's works. The related speech and work claims are not made identical.

Jesus calls the Father's command eternal life and speaks as told; Peter says Jesus has words of eternal life. Their speaker roles and Father-command/Jesus-word formulations differ without losing the explicit life-giving speech connection.

Both connect Jesus' departure from the world with going to the Father. John13's narrator adds His hour and love to the end; John16 gives Jesus' own coming-from-Father and returning statement. Neither narration is silently substituted for the other's wording.

Both connect Judas's betrayal with evil agency. John13:2 says the devil already put the intention in his heart during supper's introduction, with a later Satan-entry at13:27; Luke places Satan entering before Judas's bargain. The actions and chronology are not collapsed.
Both say the Father gave all things into the Son's hands. John13 additionally describes Jesus' knowledge of divine origin and return; John3 adds the Father's love.

Both picture the superior girding himself to serve others. John narrates Jesus taking a towel after rising from supper; Luke's parable promises a master girding and serving watchful slaves. The towel, task, people and genre differ.

Both explicitly describe washing the feet of God's people. Jesus washes and towels the disciples' feet; Timothy lists washing saints' feet among a widow's good works. The actors and settings are not identified.

Peter's question about the Lord washing his feet can be compared with Jesus' later Lord-and-Teacher explanation that He washed their feet as a pattern for mutual service. The later teaching explains the role reversal, not independent detail of Peter's words.

Jesus contrasts Peter's present nonunderstanding with promised later understanding; John12 contrasts initial nonunderstanding with later remembering of Scripture and entry actions after glorification. The parallel concerns delayed reception, while understanding and remembering, and promised versus narrated stages, remain distinct.

Both connect washing with a changed holy relationship. John makes Jesus' washing necessary for Peter's share with Him; Corinthians says you washed yourselves clean, then were sanctified and justified in Jesus' name and God's Spirit. Different agency and language are preserved without equating foot washing and a particular rite.

Both call Jesus' disciples clean. John13 uses bathing/feet language and an exception explained through the betrayer; John15 attributes cleanness to the spoken word without repeating that exception. The grounds and qualifications remain distinct.

Both explicitly describe Jesus knowing the one who would hand Him over. John13 uses that knowledge to explain not-all-clean; John6 describes knowledge from the beginning alongside unbelief. No new account of compulsion or unidentified persons is supplied.

Jesus' question about understanding what He did receives its stated example-purpose in13:15. The link interprets the narrated foot washing through His own teaching, not another independent washing account.

Both relate calling Jesus Lord to the response He expects. John affirms Teacher and Lord before His service command; Luke challenges Lord, Lord speech without doing His sayings. The title affirmation and rebuke have different settings and wording.

Jesus commands mutual foot washing after His example; Timothy names washing saints' feet as a good work. The later description offers a concrete service counterpart, not proof that every recipient reenacted this supper or that the directive had one unstated institutional form.

Both describe Christ's action as an example for followers. John concerns mutual service following foot washing; Peter concerns suffering and following His footsteps. Different acts and contexts are not conflated.

Both deny a slave being greater than the master. John also names messenger and sender in the service setting; Matthew names disciple/teacher and applies the pattern to hostile treatment. The contexts and additional analogies differ.

Both connect blessing with acting on received teaching rather than reception alone. John names knowing and doing these things; Luke names hearing God's word and keeping it. The instruction contexts and formulations remain distinct.

Both describe betrayal by a trusted table companion. John says eating My bread and lifting a heel; the actual psalm says eating my loaves and magnifying treachery. The heel image is not inserted into this supplied psalm, and Judas is not named there.
Both say Jesus tells the disciples before an event so that they believe when it occurs. John13 additionally says that I am; John14 does not repeat that object in the cited unit.
Both link receiving Jesus' messengers with receiving Jesus and the One who sent Him. John says anyone I send; Matthew addresses you. The chain is explicit without identifying every later messenger.
Both announce that one of the supper group will hand Jesus over. John describes His troubled spirit; Mark names someone eating with Him. The emotions, wording and feast chronology are not merged.

Both describe the group's disturbed uncertainty about the betrayer. John narrates exchanged looks and perplexity; Mark narrates grief and individual Surely-not-I questions. The responses are not made verbally identical.

John21 explicitly recalls the loved disciple reclining against Jesus at supper and asking about betrayal. This identifies the narrative description repeated here without assigning the unnamed disciple a name not given in these units.

The later retrospect identifies the loved supper disciple who asked about betrayal, providing a concrete counterpart for the unnamed one Peter prompts here. It does not independently narrate Peter's signal or supply a personal name for the narrative's unnamed description.

John21 explicitly recalls the chest-reclining disciple's Lord-directed betrayal question. John13 says Lord, who is it; John21 expands the question to who hands Thee over. The retrospect's wording and unidentified person remain as supplied.

Both identify the betrayer through shared food. John has Jesus dip and give a morsel to named Judas; Mark names one dipping with Him into the dish. The actions are not made identical or the recipient named within Mark's cited saying.

Both explicitly say Satan entered Judas. John places it after the morsel and adds Jesus' do-more-quickly command; Luke places it before the authorities' bargain. The different timing is not harmonized.

The group's not knowing why Jesus spoke to Judas is followed by their purchase-or-charity guesses. The next unit explains possible interpretations without establishing that either was Jesus' real purpose.

The disciples' guesses depend on Judas having the money box, the same role the narrator earlier describes. John12's theft and motive judgment is not transferred into the disciples' later thoughts or made evidence that their charity guess was true.

Judas's receiving the morsel and immediate exit follow the narrated gift and do-more-quickly command. The link identifies the sequence's stated antecedents, not independent evidence for the night notice or an unquoted mission.
Both announce the Son of Man's glorification. John13 says now after Judas leaves and names God glorified in Him; John12 names the arriving hour. Their stage and wording are not collapsed.

Both connect the Son's and Father's glorification. John13 speaks of God glorifying Him in Himself at once; John17 requests the Son's glory so that He may glorify the Father. The condition, request and temporal forms are preserved.

Jesus expressly recalls the where-I-go-you-cannot-come saying previously addressed to the Jews. John7 gives the earlier little-time and seek/not-find language; John13 now addresses disciples. Audience and where-I-am/go wording are not silently made identical.
Both command loving one another after Jesus' love. John13 calls it new; John15 states This is My commandment. No additional historical theory of the word new is imposed.

Both present mutual love as evidence of relationship to Jesus or spiritual life. John13 concerns everyone recognizing His disciples; the letter concerns knowing passage from death into life through brotherly love. Observers, claims and warnings differ.

Jesus' promise that Peter will follow later can be compared with His later Follow Me command after a prediction of Peter's death. John21's narrator interprets that prediction as death glorifying God; it does not settle every meaning or exact execution method of the earlier promise.

Both give Peter's expressed readiness for death, but John says he will lay down his life for Jesus, while Mark says even if he must die with Him he will not deny Him. In John, Peter also asks why he cannot follow now; Mark places the insistence after the denial prediction. The relation words and speech sequence remain distinct.

Both predict three denials before cockcrow. John first questions Peter's life-laying pledge and does not say twice; Mark specifies this night and two crows. No crow-count or timing reconciliation is invented.

Both tell the disciples not to let their hearts be troubled. The opening joins belief in God and Jesus; the later assurance gives Jesus' peace and forbids fear. The repeated comfort does not make every clause identical.

Both describe a divinely prepared future home. Jesus speaks of His Father's house and preparing dwelling places; Hebrews names God preparing a city for those desiring a heavenly country. The metaphors, recipients and descriptions of preparation are not converted into an architectural map.

Both anticipate followers being with the coming Lord. John names prepared place and Jesus receiving them to Himself; Paul names resurrection, clouds and meeting Him. The passages are compared without assigning one meaning or chronology to every coming saying in John14.

The statement that they know the way is clarified by Jesus' I-am-the-way answer following Thomas's objection. The answer concerns coming to the Father through Jesus, not a supplied geographical route to dwelling places.

Both disciples ask about Jesus' destination. Thomas links not knowing where He goes with not knowing the way; Peter asks where and receives a cannot-follow-now promise. The disciples, questions and answers remain distinct.

Both present access to the Father through Jesus. John names Jesus way, truth and life and says no one comes except through Him; Ephesians names both groups' access through Him in one Spirit. The Spirit and group descriptions are not inserted into John's sentence.
Both connect knowing Jesus with knowing His Father. John14 adds now knowing and seeing; John8 rebukes questioners who know neither. Their positive promise and negative rebuke remain distinct.

Both request a divine disclosure. Philip asks Jesus to show the Father; Moses asks the Lord to show His glory and receives a response about glory and the impossibility of seeing His face and living. Revealer, request object and resulting words are not equated.

Both connect seeing Jesus with seeing His Father or Sender. John14 answers named Philip and his request; John12 gives the shorter beholding-the-Sender saying. The statements do not erase the Father/Son distinction.

Both deny Jesus speaking from Himself and connect His speech with the Father. John14 adds reciprocal indwelling and the Father's works; John12 describes the Father's command about what to say. Speech, work and command formulations remain distinct.

Both appeal to the works as grounds for recognizing Father/Son indwelling even when the speaker is not believed. John10 adds the conditional failure-to-do-Father's-works clause; John14 directly commands belief.

Acts narrates many signs and healings through apostles after Jesus' ministry, providing concrete followers' works to compare. It does not quantify greater, identify every believer's work, or turn the crowd's hoped-for shadow contact into the stated cause of every healing.

Both promise response to asking in Jesus' name. John14 says Jesus will do it for the Father's glorification in the Son; John16 explicitly names the Father as giver. Their stated agents and purpose clauses are preserved.

Both relate requests in Jesus' name to promised response. John14 explicitly says ask Me and I will do it; John16 names asking the Father and His giving. Neither address or agent is silently rewritten to match the other.

Both connect love with keeping commandments. Jesus says loving Me leads to keeping My commands; the letter describes love of God as keeping His commands and adds they are not burdensome. The pronouns, addressed persons and added claim remain distinct.

Both promise the Advocate for the disciples. John14 has Jesus ask and the Father give another Advocate forever; John16 has Jesus send Him upon departing. The sending/giving roles and departure condition are not collapsed.

Both name the Spirit of truth. John14 contrasts the world's inability to receive Him with disciples' knowledge and indwelling promise; John15 names proceeding from the Father, Jesus' sending and witness to Him. The distinct relations and tasks are preserved.

Both assure disciples of Jesus' continuing presence. John says He will not leave them orphans and is coming to them; Matthew says He is with them through the age's consummation. The formulations do not determine an unmentioned date for every Johannine coming promise.

Both connect followers' life with Jesus' life. John14 says because I live you will live and contrasts world/disciple sight; John6 connects the living Sender, Jesus and the eater who lives because of Him. The eating image and visibility clauses remain distinct.

Both passages describe the Father-Son-followers indwelling relation. John14 says Jesus is in the Father and the disciples in Jesus and Jesus in them; John17 additionally says the Father is in Jesus and prays for unity and the world's belief and knowledge. The directions, petitions and predicted recognition remain distinct.

Both connect love, keeping Jesus' teaching and the Father's love. The first promises Jesus' self-revelation; the later answer promises Father and Son making their dwelling with the person. The related promises remain their stated forms.

Both question Jesus' manifestation to the world. Judas explicitly not Iscariot asks why revelation to the disciples rather than the world; His brothers earlier urged a public display. Their persons, motives and stated requests are not equated.

Both connect keeping divine teaching with indwelling. Jesus promises Father and Son dwelling with the one loving and keeping His word; the letter describes commandment keeping, mutual abiding and the given Spirit as assurance. The explicit persons and conditions remain distinct.

Both refer Jesus' speech to the Father who sent Him rather than autonomous speech. John14 adds lack of love and failure to keep His words; John12 describes the Father's command. The moral contrast is not supplied as though present in the target.

Jesus' words spoken while with the disciples are the stated subject the coming Advocate will remind them of. The following promise supplies a future remembrance relation, not independent evidence for every present speech or an identity of the two teachers.

Both promise the Spirit's instruction. John14 names the Father sending the Holy Spirit in Jesus' name and remembering His words; John16 names guidance into truth, heard speech and announced coming things. Those agents, relations and tasks are not made verbally identical.

Both promise peace in Jesus amid the world's contrasting condition. John14 names His gift and fearless hearts; John16 names affliction and His victory. The sayings do not deny the stated affliction or repeat identical promises.

Both describe Jesus going to the Father. John14 also recalls coming again and says the Father is greater than I; John16 states coming from the Father into the world and leaving it. The greater-than wording is retained, not inserted into the target or explained away.
